subject: history_social
passage: Cookbooks printed in the early 1800s commonly tell the reader to add "a handful of flour" or "butter the size of a walnut" and to bake "in a quick oven until done." By the end of the century, many cookbooks gave level cup and spoon measurements, oven temperatures, and cooking times to the minute. Historians of food have sometimes attributed the change to the arrival of new kitchen tools. Historian Grace Mbeki points out, however, that a vague instruction is perfectly usable by a cook who has learned by watching others, and that the new cookbooks were marketed explicitly to women setting up kitchens far from the families in which they had grown up. In her view, the shift toward precise measurement mainly reflects ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: a readership that could no longer rely on having been taught in person.
choices.B: the invention of the measuring cup and the oven thermometer.
choices.C: a decline in the skill of professional cooks over the course of the 1800s.
choices.D: a preference among all cooks for exact recipes once such recipes became available.

explanation.why: Mbeki offers two linked observations: vague instructions suffice for a cook trained by watching others, and the precise new cookbooks were aimed at readers who had moved away from the families that would have trained them. Put together, the precision made up for missing in-person instruction, which is the explanation she prefers to the one about tools.
explanation.A: Correct. Vague recipes work for cooks trained by watching; the new books were sold to readers who had left such training behind, so precision replaced what those readers lacked.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is the explanation other historians offer and the one Mbeki argues against.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text discusses home cooks and their readers, not professional cooks, and never mentions a decline in skill.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Mbeki ties the change to one particular group of readers; the text does not claim that every cook preferred precision.
